header: Reading a health check-up roster with Gemini. I split the work the way each part is done best:
* the WORDS of the rows (serial, ticket, name, department code, department) are read by two Gemini models (a primary and a checker) from the whole page image, as JSON;

* the DATES are read by Gemini from a clean crop of each merged date cell (a few digits, so a cheap model reads them; a stronger one is asked when the first reading is not a date of the schedule's month);

* the GEOMETRY decides which rows sit under which date: the ruled lines of the table (rosterGeometry.ts, image analysis, no OCR). A model asked for the date of every row misplaces the rows at the edge of a group; the rules of the table do not.

My checks (any warning means the schedule is NOT stored and a person looks at it): the two readers must find the same number of rows; the table must have as many ruled rows as the readers found; a printed date must be a date of the schedule's month; groups of an odd size; dates out of order; the SL.NO sequence. I keep a different ticket or department code read by the checker as an alternative reading, so that the HR directory can confirm one of them.

symbols.returns: { centers: number[]; divided: number; surplus: number; dataTop: number }
doc: Finds which ruled interval each row of the reading sits in. The table's heading rows (title, column names) lie ABOVE the first data row, and the date column shows where that is: the heading is a closed cell (or two) at the top of the date column with no date in it, and the first cell with a date starts at the first data row (a cell open at the top is a group carried over a page break, never a heading). Intervals above that point are not data. Where a rule is missing (rows with no line between them) one interval holds several rows, so I divide the interval whose pieces would be tallest, again and again, until the number of intervals equals the number of rows the readers found. Returns the vertical centre of every row, how many rows had to be made by dividing, and how many intervals were left over at the bottom.
